newsitem.title: USA: US 30-, 15-year mortgage rates rise in week.
newsitem.headline: US 30-, 15-year mortgage rates rise in week.

text.p: The average commitment rate on U.S. 30-year fixed-rate mortgages rose to 7.57 percent in the week ending December 13 after falling for seven consecutive weeks, the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp said Thursday. Last week's 30-year rate was 7.44 percent.
Fifteen-year loans also rose to an average 7.06 percent in the week after falling seven weeks in a row. Last week's 15-year rate averaged 6.96 percent.
Adjustable rate mortgages inched upward to an average 5.52 percent from 5.47 percent last week, Freddie Mac said.
A year ago, the 30-year rate averaged 7.15 percent, the 15-year 6.71 percent, and the ARM 5.55 percent.

"This week's release of the consumer and producer price indices for the month of November showed the producer price index rising four tenths of a percent, which made the market a little nervous about inflation and pushed interest rates up slightly," Frank Nothaft, Freddie Mac deputy chief economist, said.
"However, the results of the indices, less the volative figures for food and energy, show inflation remains in check," Nothaft added.

Earlier Thursday the Labor Department said that U.S. November consumer prices rose 0.3 percent, but excluding food and energy were up only 0.2 percent. The department said Wednesday that U.S. producer prices excluding food and energy fell 0.3 percent last month.
Also, last week Labor reported a 118,000 increase in U.S. November non-farm payrolls and a jobless rate of 5.4 percent.

Freddie Mac said lenders charged an average 1.7 percent in fees and points on 30- and 15-year loans, both unchanged from last week. They charged 1.4 percent on the ARM, up from 1.3 percent the prior week.
